## Introduction

Combines type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillation measurements to map
two-dimensional confidence regions in the $(\Omega_c, w)$ plane with
`numcosmo_py`[^numcosmo_py] and `plotnine`.

A confidence region can be obtained either from the likelihood surface itself,
through a likelihood-ratio test, or by approximating that surface with a
Gaussian centred on the best fit. Here the two answers differ by a large
factor, and most of the difference comes not from the likelihood being
non-Gaussian but from which information matrix is used to build the
approximation. `fisher_border` uses the covariance ellipse; `conf_region`
evaluates the likelihood-ratio contour and profiles any nuisance parameters.

The underlying fitting workflow is introduced in
[Supernova Type Ia Analysis](snia.qmd) and is assumed below.

## Combining Datasets

A `Dataset` holds an arbitrary collection of data objects. Since the likelihood is a sum
of $-2\ln L$ contributions, heterogeneous probes are combined simply by appending them to
the same container. We join the Union2.1 supernova compilation with two BAO measurements,
one at low redshift from the 6dF Galaxy Survey and one at $z \approx 1.5$ from BOSS
quasars.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

from numcosmo_py import Nc, Ncm

# Initialize the library
Ncm.cfg_init()

# Dark energy model with a constant equation of state.
cosmo = Nc.HICosmoDEXcdm()

# Change the parameterization and enforce spatial flatness, so that the dark
# energy density follows from the closure relation instead of being fitted.
cosmo.omega_x2omega_k()
cosmo["Omegak"] = 0.0

cosmo["H0"] = 70.0
cosmo["Omegab"] = 0.05
cosmo["Omegac"] = 0.25
cosmo["Tgamma0"] = 2.72
cosmo["w"] = -1.0

mset = Ncm.MSet.new_array([cosmo])

# Free parameters: the cold dark matter density and the equation of state.
cosmo.props.Omegac_fit = True
cosmo.props.w_fit = True
mset.prepare_fparam_map()

mset.pretty_log()
```

The distance object is shared by every probe, so the background is computed once and
reused.

```{python}
dist = Nc.Distance(zf=2.5)

dset = Ncm.Dataset.new_array(
    [
        Nc.DataDistMu.new_from_id(dist, Nc.DataSNIAId.SIMPLE_UNION2_1),
        Nc.data_bao_create(dist, Nc.DataBaoId.RDV_BEUTLER2011),
        Nc.data_bao_create(dist, Nc.DataBaoId.RDV_BOSS_QSO_ATA2017),
    ]
)

lh = Ncm.Likelihood(dataset=dset)
```

::: {.callout-note}
NumCosmo also provides BAO likelihoods given as tabulated $-2\ln p$ curves, such as
`EMPIRICAL_FIT_ROSS2015`. These carry no Gaussian mean vector, so no Fisher matrix can be
built from them. Since everything below relies on the Fisher matrix, the combination here
is restricted to likelihoods with an explicit mean.
:::

## Fitting the Model

We minimize $-2\ln L$ with the derivative-free Nelder--Mead algorithm from NLOPT and then
compute the parameter covariance.

```{python}
fit = Ncm.Fit.factory(
    Ncm.FitType.NLOPT, "ln-neldermead", lh, mset, Ncm.FitGradType.NUMDIFF_FORWARD
)

fit.run(Ncm.FitRunMsgs.SIMPLE)
fit.log_info()

fit.fisher()
fit.log_covar()
```

## Confidence Regions

The `LHRatio2d` object maps out regions for a chosen pair of parameters. It requires a fit
that has converged to its best fit and that already carries a covariance, which is why
`Ncm.Fit.fisher` is called before it is constructed.

```{python}
lhr2d = Ncm.LHRatio2d.new(
    fit,
    mset.fparam_get_pi_by_name("Omegac"),
    mset.fparam_get_pi_by_name("w"),
    1.0e-3,
)
```

Two methods are then available. `fisher_border` returns the ellipse implied by the
covariance matrix, that is, the quadratic approximation to $-2\ln L$ around the minimum.
`conf_region` instead traces the contour where the likelihood ratio reaches the threshold
for the requested confidence level, evaluating the likelihood itself at every boundary
point and assuming nothing about its shape.

Two remarks on `conf_region`. When parameters other than the two being scanned are left
free, it minimizes over them at each boundary point, so that the contour is a profile
likelihood; in this example $\Omega_c$ and $w$ are the only free parameters, so no inner
minimization is required and the calculation is correspondingly cheap. And for two
parameters the $68.27\%$ level corresponds to $\Delta\chi^2 = 2.30$ rather than $1$, a
conversion handled internally from the confidence level.

```{python}
levels = [
    (Ncm.C.stats_1sigma(), r"1$\sigma$"),
    (Ncm.C.stats_2sigma(), r"2$\sigma$"),
    (Ncm.C.stats_3sigma(), r"3$\sigma$"),
]

lh_pd_list, expected_pd_list = [], []

# Largest region first, so that the nested fills stack sensibly.
for clevel, name in reversed(levels):
    lh_rg = lhr2d.conf_region(clevel, 300.0, Ncm.FitRunMsgs.NONE)
    fisher_rg = lhr2d.fisher_border(clevel, 300.0, Ncm.FitRunMsgs.NONE)

    lh_pd_list.append(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "Omegac": np.array(lh_rg.p1.dup_array()),
                "w": np.array(lh_rg.p2.dup_array()),
                "sigma": name,
            }
        )
    )
    expected_pd_list.append(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "Omegac": np.array(fisher_rg.p1.dup_array()),
                "w": np.array(fisher_rg.p2.dup_array()),
                "sigma": name,
                "information": "Expected",
                "border": f"expected {name}",
            }
        )
    )

lh_pd = pd.concat(lh_pd_list)
expected_pd = pd.concat(expected_pd_list)
best_fit_pd = pd.DataFrame({"Omegac": [cosmo["Omegac"]], "w": [cosmo["w"]]})
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-lhratio-vs-fisher
# | fig-cap: >
# |   Confidence regions in the $(\Omega_c, w)$ plane at 1, 2 and 3$\sigma$. Filled
# |   areas are the likelihood-ratio regions; the lines are the Gaussian (Fisher)
# |   approximation from the expected information, which is visibly too small.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

(
    ggplot(lh_pd, aes("Omegac", "w", fill="sigma"))
    + geom_polygon(alpha=0.30)
    + geom_path(
        data=expected_pd,
        mapping=aes("Omegac", "w", group="border", linetype="information"),
        inherit_aes=False,
    )
    + geom_point(
        data=best_fit_pd, mapping=aes("Omegac", "w"), inherit_aes=False, size=3
    )
    + labs(x=r"$\Omega_c$", y=r"$w$", fill="Confidence", linetype="Method")
    + doc_theme()
)
```

The ellipses are clearly too small. Comparing the enclosed areas puts a number on it.

```{python}
def region_area(frame):
    """Area enclosed by a closed contour, from the shoelace formula."""
    x = frame["Omegac"].to_numpy()
    y = frame["w"].to_numpy()
    return 0.5 * abs(np.dot(x, np.roll(y, 1)) - np.dot(y, np.roll(x, 1)))


for _, name in levels:
    area_lh = region_area(lh_pd[lh_pd["sigma"] == name])
    area_ex = region_area(expected_pd[expected_pd["sigma"] == name])
    print(f"{name}: likelihood ratio / expected information = {area_lh / area_ex:.3f}")
```

## Expected and Observed Information

The ratio is close to $1.8$ and, more tellingly, barely changes between $1\sigma$ and
$3\sigma$. That rules out non-Gaussianity as the main cause: a quadratic approximation
degrades as one moves away from the minimum, so a shape effect would grow with the
confidence level rather than staying flat.

The explanation lies in which information matrix `Ncm.Fit.fisher` computes. It returns the
*expected* information, an average of the curvature of $-2\ln L$ over hypothetical
realizations of the data drawn from the model. The likelihood-ratio contour, in contrast,
responds to the *observed* information, the curvature of $-2\ln L$ at this particular best
fit with these particular residuals. The two agree when the model is linear in its
parameters, or when it describes the data perfectly, and otherwise they need not.

`Ncm.Fit.obs_fisher` computes the observed version. It must be called only after every
`LHRatio2d` calculation is finished, since it leaves the fit state without its best-fit
flag. The corresponding ellipse is then built directly from the covariance matrix, using
the fact that for two parameters the $\chi^2$ threshold inverts in closed form,
$\Delta\chi^2 = -2\ln(1 - P)$.

```{python}
fit.obs_fisher()
fit.log_covar()

covar = fit.get_covar()
covar_obs = np.array([[covar.get(i, j) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)])

centre_a = np.array([cosmo["Omegac"], cosmo["w"]])
cholesky = np.linalg.cholesky(covar_obs)
theta_a = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, 300)
unit_circle_a = np.vstack([np.cos(theta_a), np.sin(theta_a)])

observed_pd_list = []
for clevel, name in reversed(levels):
    points_a = centre_a[:, None] + np.sqrt(-2.0 * np.log1p(-clevel)) * (
        cholesky @ unit_circle_a
    )
    observed_pd_list.append(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "Omegac": points_a[0],
                "w": points_a[1],
                "sigma": name,
                "information": "Observed",
                "border": f"observed {name}",
            }
        )
    )

observed_pd = pd.concat(observed_pd_list)
border_pd = pd.concat([expected_pd, observed_pd])
```

```{python}
# | label: fig-confidence-regions
# | fig-cap: >
# |   Likelihood ratio regions (filled) with the ellipses built from the expected and
# |   from the observed information.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

(
    ggplot(lh_pd, aes("Omegac", "w", fill="sigma"))
    + geom_polygon(alpha=0.30)
    + geom_path(
        data=border_pd,
        mapping=aes("Omegac", "w", group="border", linetype="information"),
        inherit_aes=False,
    )
    + geom_point(
        data=best_fit_pd, mapping=aes("Omegac", "w"), inherit_aes=False, size=3
    )
    + labs(x=r"$\Omega_c$", y=r"$w$", fill="Confidence", linetype="Information")
    + doc_theme()
)
```

The observed-information ellipses land almost on top of the likelihood-ratio regions.

```{python}
for _, name in levels:
    area_lh = region_area(lh_pd[lh_pd["sigma"] == name])
    area_ex = region_area(expected_pd[expected_pd["sigma"] == name])
    area_ob = region_area(observed_pd[observed_pd["sigma"] == name])
    print(
        f"{name}: likelihood ratio / expected = {area_lh / area_ex:.3f}, "
        f"likelihood ratio / observed = {area_lh / area_ob:.3f}"
    )
```

This separates the two effects cleanly. The choice of information matrix accounts for a
factor of roughly $1.8$ that is the same at every confidence level, while the
non-Gaussianity of the likelihood accounts for the small remainder, which grows from
under one per cent at $1\sigma$ to a few per cent at $3\sigma$ exactly as a failing
quadratic approximation should. Practically, quoting errors from the expected information
would understate the uncertainty on $w$ by about twenty per cent, for a reason unrelated
to the shape of the likelihood.

## Conclusion

We combined supernova and BAO data into a single likelihood, fitted a flat dark energy
model, and compared confidence regions obtained from the likelihood-ratio test with the
Gaussian approximations built from the expected and from the observed information. All
three are frequentist constructions describing the coverage of the region under repeated
sampling, unlike the credible regions produced by the MCMC analysis at the end of
[Supernova Type Ia Analysis](snia.qmd).

Both the model and the data can be extended from here. Cosmic chronometer measurements of
$H(z)$, available through `Nc.DataHubble`, constrain the expansion rate directly and pair
naturally with treating $H_0$ as a free parameter; note that any additional free parameter
turns each boundary point of `conf_region` into a minimization, which raises the cost of
the calculation considerably.
